behavior_change: A session that edits any `.claude/agents/*.md` must now leave a `data/proposals/PROP-*.json` on disk naming that file and carrying a verdict, or `check_collab.py --staged` (postlude 1e) exits 1, the Stop hook nudges once, and the CI `collab` job opens an issue; the observable in a future run is a PROP file per contract edit and an `Actor:` trailer on the commit that carries it.
checks_touched: tools/validate.py:check_actor (new; WARNING-only unless --strict-actors, so it cannot fail a run as shipped)
tools/check_collab.py:check_changes CRAFT branch (new; the only thing that makes the review non-optional)
tools/check_collab.py:prop_covers (new; the whole strength of the CRAFT gate reduces to this four-line function)
.claude/hooks/collab-gate.py:on_stop (new; the only gate anywhere that checks a PROP's date)
.github/workflows/ci.yml:collab (new; the only control a session cannot switch off from inside)
cost_if_wrong: Six weeks out, `data/proposals/` holds a row of ADOPTs with `survives: true` on every challenge and `ruling: null` on every file. The agent contracts have drifted the way this file says instruction changes always drift, and each drift is covered by a receipt that satisfies every gate. The repo will look more governed than before and be exactly as governed, because the gates check that a JSON file exists and never that a review happened. Second cost, already live: `data/taste.md` and `data/chains/_archetypes.md` are now CONSTITUTION-tier, so a `yotam` session cannot complete `run radar` or `run chain` at all.
how_you_would_know: Three greps, none of which any command currently runs: the fraction of challenges across `data/proposals/` with `survives: false` (a run of all-true is the tell), the count of PROPs whose `actor` equals the author of the change they cover, and the count with `ruling: null` older than a month. Nothing in CLAUDE.md, `check health` or `run review` reads any of them today, and this contract forbids the surface that would. That is a REJECT-level answer by this file's own rule at line 88, and it is the narrowing below rather than a REJECT only because the fix is one row in a table, not a new script.

challenges.claim: The blind list at lines 45-71 is a constraint rather than a posture, because it is 'a list, not a posture'.
challenges.attack: Writing the list down does not make it checkable. Nothing on disk records what the reviewing session read: a PROP carries no session id, no transcript reference, no diff sha, and no field distinguishing 'spawned in fresh context with the diff' from 'the authoring session continuing its own turn with the whole rationale in scope'. `v_proposal` reads none of it, `check_collab.py` reads only `files` and `verdict`. The peer precedent does not rescue it either: `run redteam` at least has `check_analyst.py` asserting a `pre_mortem` block exists and that FINAL implies a complete `red_team`, so a skipped red team leaves a hole in the artifact. A skipped blind list leaves an artifact that is byte-identical to an honest one. The list is the most honest paragraph in the file and it is still unfalsifiable.

challenges.claim: Owning no calibration surface is right, because 'a calibration surface for a decision that fires a handful of times a year is ceremony, not learning' (lines 23-26).
challenges.attack: The refusal of a `cass_calibrate.py` is correct and I would not build one. The refusal that does not survive is the one smuggled in beside it: Cass is the only agent in this repo that does not read its own prior record. Nell's contract opens 'data/radar/scout-log.json — my own log. First, always.' Atlas opens with `_map-log.json`, Stocky with `_dive-log.json`, and this file's own 'I read' table (line 60) demands that of the agent under review — 'that agent's own log ... whether the record supports the change's premise'. `data/proposals/` is absent from that table. The ground truth already exists and costs nothing to read: `ruling` is Ron's verdict on the verdict, and `check_collab.py --brief` already prints open PROPs. A reviewer that never reads the rulings on its past reviews cannot notice it has been overruled three times on the same axis. That is not ceremony, it is the single cheapest learning loop in the repo, and this is the only contract that declines it.

challenges.claim: A PROP file is the receipt that an instruction change was attacked before it landed (line 32-41, and CLAUDE.md's CRAFT tier row).
challenges.attack: Tested, not argued. I staged an edit to `.claude/agents/nell-scanner.md` alongside a PROP dated 2026-08-01 with `actor: yotam`, no `reviewed_by` key at all, three identical placeholder challenges all `survives: true`, and `surviving_objection: "none really"`. `check_collab.py --staged` printed `check_collab: OK`, exit 0. `v_proposal` returned zero errors and zero warnings. `data/proposals/` is DATA tier, so the author writes it freely; `prop_covers` (check_collab.py:225-230) tests only `verdict in VERDICTS` and `path in files`; `reviewed_by` is read by no gate in the repo (grep across tools/, .claude/hooks/, .github/ returns nothing). Neither the postlude gate nor CI checks the PROP's date, so one PROP naming a file in August satisfies every edit to that file forever. The one gate that checks the date is the Stop hook, which is a single nudge, fires only where repo hooks fire, and is blind to subagent writes (`from_tool_use` returns `([], [])` for `Agent`/`Task`, and `.claude/settings.json` registers no `SubagentStop`) — which is how every agent in this repo actually writes. The receipt is real; nothing verifies a purchase was made.

challenges.claim: The four attacks at lines 75-89 are the substance of the review, and CLAUDE.md's new `run devil` row states they are 'Machine-checked by `v_proposal` in `tools/validate.py`'.
challenges.attack: `v_proposal`'s required keys are id, as_of, actor, files, verdict, challenges, surviving_objection. `behavior_change`, `checks_touched`, `cost_if_wrong` and `how_you_would_know` appear in this contract's own JSON skeleton at lines 108-111 and are required by nothing. So attacks 1, 2 and 4 — including the one this file calls 'the highest-value question in this repo' — are documented, not enforced, and a PROP that omits all three validates clean. The `challenges` check counts to three and type-checks a boolean; it cannot distinguish three attacks from three copies of one sentence. That is precisely the pattern line 82 names as worse than removal: 'a change that makes a check unfalsifiable — one that can no longer fail'. The file says the repo has shipped that bug twice. This is the third, shipped inside the artifact whose job is to catch it. Adjacent instance in the same diff: `check_actor` is warning-only unless `--strict-actors`, which nothing passes, so as shipped it cannot fail for the case it was built for; that one at least follows the `--strict-citations` precedent and names its backfill, but no gate or date will ever force the flip.

challenges.claim: 'I refuse reviewing a change I wrote' (lines 137-140), with the first PROP carved out as reviewed by an instance given the diff and none of the argument.
challenges.attack: The refusal has no mechanism and the carve-out is the author granting themselves the one exemption that matters, in the document that establishes the rule. This PROP is the proof: it declares `actor: ron` and `reviewed_by: cass-adversary`, both self-declared strings, in a repo where the file's own two-venue section concedes that identity inside the repo is a claim. The `github.actor` backstop does not reach here — it reconciles who pushed against the `Actor:` trailer, not who reviewed against who authored, and it is asymmetric by design, so `Actor: ron` pushed by Ron is never questioned. The clause is worth keeping as a norm, but the file should say it is a norm with no enforcement, in the same voice it uses for 'identity here is declared, not proven'. Stating an unenforceable rule flatly, twelve lines after modelling exactly the right way to state an unenforceable rule, is the one place this document forgets its own register.

challenges.claim: 'I am not a permission step. A REJECT from me does not stop anyone' (lines 18-21).
challenges.attack: Half true, and the half that is false is load-bearing. Cass's verdict is not a permission step — correct, and the right design. But the EXISTENCE of a PROP is one: `check_collab.py`'s CRAFT branch hard-fails the postlude and CI when a contract changes with no PROP naming it, and the Stop hook refuses the session's first attempt to end. So `run devil` is mandatory even though its outcome is not binding. That is the correct place to put the teeth, and it is why this survives: the gate asserts that a review happened, never that it approved, which is exactly the distinction the file is defending. What does not survive is the wording — `docs/friend-guide.md` tells Yotam 'a REJECT does not stop you' without saying that a missing PROP does, and a collaborator who reads only that line will be surprised by his first blocked Stop.

challenges.claim: The gap being covered is real: 'the class of change whose effect is invisible at the moment it lands' (lines 30-41).
challenges.attack: I tried to break the diagnosis and could not. Every other artifact in the repo does announce its own quality through a gate: chains through `check_chain.py`, dives through `check_analyst.py`, everything through `validate.py`. An instruction change passes all of them by construction, and the worked example — softening one evidence sentence in `nell-scanner.md` and seeing the damage six weeks later as 'the world got harder' — is the true shape of the failure. The nearest counter is that `scout_calibrate.py`, `map_calibrate.py` and the shadow book already measure output quality over time and would eventually show drift; but they attribute it to the world, not to a diff, which is the entire point being made. The premise is sound. Everything wrong with this change is in the enforcement, not the reasoning.

surviving_objection: This contract exempts itself from the one discipline it exists to impose, and claims a machine backstop it does not have. Every peer agent must read its own prior record first, and this file's own 'I read' table demands that of the agent under review — yet `data/proposals/` is absent from that table and lines 23-26 forbid the surface that would supply it, so a reviewer that has been overruled three times on the same axis cannot notice. Meanwhile CLAUDE.md's new `run devil` row says the four attacks are 'Machine-checked by `v_proposal`', and three of the four are not required keys, so a PROP carrying only a verdict and three copies of one sentence validates clean and satisfies both the postlude gate and CI. Narrow it two ways and it is right: add `data/proposals/*.json` with a non-null `ruling` to the 'I read' table as the first row, the way Nell reads scout-log first, and make `behavior_change`, `checks_touched`, `cost_if_wrong` and `how_you_would_know` required keys in `v_proposal` so the contract's own skeleton is the enforced shape. Neither costs a script. Without them the honest reading of this change is that it is a norm with a receipt, and the file should say so in the same register it uses for 'identity here is declared, not proven', because that sentence is the best thing in the document and the standard the rest of it should be held to.

changelog.change: First review. Read the diff, the standing contracts and the gates; no rationale, ledger prose or transcript. Tested the CRAFT gate against a stale self-authored rubber-stamp PROP and it passed. ADOPT_NARROWED on two concrete clauses.

ADOPT_NARROWED acted on, both narrowings applied: (1) .claude/agents/cass-adversary.md now reads ruled PROPs first, as the first row of its own I-read table; (2) tools/validate.py v_proposal now requires reviewed_by=cass-adversary and non-empty behavior_change, checks_touched, cost_if_wrong, how_you_would_know, plus 3 DISTINCT challenge claims. The reviewer's own bypass fixture (PROP dated 2026-08-01, placeholder challenges, no reviewed_by) now fails validation with 7 errors. Machinery defects 1-5 and 9-10 from the same review also fixed; 6-8 recorded as open.
